page.title: tinyactors compared with Rivet
page.description: Who places an actor, what a sleeping one keeps, how its tests move time, what a deploy does to running actors, and when Rivet Actors are the better choice.

hero.headline: Actors in your backend, with no control plane
hero.lede: Rivet runs one actor per agent session in your Node.js or Bun backend, placed by Rivet Cloud or a control plane you deploy. tinyactors runs each session as a statechart in your process, with nothing beside it. Choose Rivet when actors must move between machines on their own.

section.heading: Rivet places actors; your program places hosts
section.p: Both run your actors in your backend's process. The difference is what runs beside it. And who decides where an actor lives.

claim.statement: Rivet's control plane places each actor
claim.p: Rivet calls its actors isolated, durable processes that run in your backend. You deploy the control plane yourself, or use Rivet Cloud.
The platform may move an actor to another node, for example when its node stops during a deploy.

claim.statement: A tinyactors actor stays in its host
claim.p: new Host(charts, options) runs the actors inside the process that imports the package. An actor stays in the host that spawned it.
A chart reaches the model's API or your database only through handlers you give the host.
claim.source: Home, "The chart decides, your code acts"
Other systems, "Give each host a system name"

section.p: There's nothing to operate. There's also nothing that moves an actor for you: which host runs where, and how a message reaches another host, is your program's code.

section.heading: A sleeping actor keeps what was stored
section.p: Most sessions sit idle between a user's messages. Their state must survive until the next one, without holding memory meanwhile.

claim.statement: A Rivet actor keeps its SQLite database
claim.p: After 30 seconds without activity an actor sleeps, and the next request wakes it. Its c.vars are never saved.
What must survive goes in c.db, a SQLite database per actor whose every committed write is replicated before it's acknowledged.

claim.statement: A hibernated actor goes to your store whole
claim.p: Give the host a store and a bound, and it writes the actors past the bound into the store: variables, active states and all. The next event wakes one.
A blob wakes only in the host that made it, or in one restored from that host's snapshot.
claim.source: Hibernation, "Cap how many actors stay in memory"
Hibernation, "Wake each blob where it was made"

section.p: Two million actors ran with at most 1000 in memory and the rest in SQLite (). An actor's data your business must keep belongs in your own database, as with any process.

section.heading: Test a thousand timeouts in one program
section.p: A session's bugs hide in what happens when an answer is late. This payment charges a card, charges again after 30 seconds without an answer and gives up after three charges:
The test's stand-in provider answers at once, 45 seconds late or never. A simulated clock jumps to each timeout, so a thousand payments run in one Node.js process:

claim.statement: Rivet's tests wait for real schedules
claim.p: setupTest starts your registry in test mode. Rivet's docs say Vitest's fake timers don't advance RivetKit's scheduler.
They recommend a short schedule and polling the result with expect.poll.

claim.statement: A simulated clock moves when tests move it
claim.p: The test above is a host, a clock and a stand-in object. Every timer of every actor waits for clock.increment().
claim.source: Testing, "Replace the chart's services and its clock"

section.heading: Ship new rules to running sessions
section.p: You deploy a turn limit while thousands of sessions are mid-conversation. Each one must keep the turns it already counted.

claim.statement: A Rivet deploy stops actors on old nodes
claim.p: Each deploy sets a version that only increases. Once a newer node connects, the old deploy gets no new actors.
With draining on, old actors stop as in a node shutdown, each with up to 15 seconds to save its state. Each deploy must read the state the last one wrote.

claim.statement: A migration moves running actors to a version
claim.p: host.addImage() adds the new chart to the running host, and host.migrate() moves actors to it.
Each keeps its active states, queue and delayed sends. The new chart reads the old variables from one event.
claim.source: Migration, "Move the actors and carry their variables"

section.p: Ten thousand agent sessions answer three prompts each, with at most 100 in memory. Version 2 adds a limit of three turns, and one migration moves every session, hibernated ones included:
No process restarted. Every session kept its count, so each one ended at the limit instead of asking the model again.

section.heading: A crash keeps what was written down
section.p: A machine dies halfway through a session. What comes back is what reached storage, and Rivet operates more of that storage for you.

claim.statement: Rivet keeps the database, not the memory
claim.p: The database survives the actor moving to another node. The sleep hook may not run in a crash, and a snapshot to SQLite on an interval loses what came after it.
A run workflow resumes from its last completed step after a crash.

claim.statement: A crash keeps what your program saved
claim.p: Actors live in your process's memory, so a crash stops them all. Hibernated actors in your store and the last snapshot come back.
Inputs after that snapshot return when your program journaled them.
claim.source: When to use tinyactors, "A crash stops memory and keeps saved state"

section.heading: Choose tinyactors for one process you understand

item.term: Nothing to operate beside your backend
item.text: The host is a library in your Node.js, Bun or Python process, so tests and production create it the same way.

item.term: Deploys that keep each session's place
item.text: A migration moves running sessions to new rules with their states, queues and timers.
A simulated clock jumps to each deadline, so one program checks a thousand sessions.

item.term: Logic an agent can write and you can read
item.text: Each session is one SCXML chart, and an uploaded chart runs in the QuickJS sandbox.

section.heading: Choose Rivet when actors must move between machines

item.term: Placement and failover you don't write
item.text: The control plane places each actor and moves it when its node stops. tinyactors leaves placement and failover between hosts to your program.
Each actor's SQLite writes are replicated before they're acknowledged, and the database follows the actor to another node.
Rivet Cloud runs the control plane on AWS and Google Cloud, or in your own VPC on AWS, Google Cloud or Azure.
A Rivet actor is a set of actions in TypeScript or Rust (Rivet, "Actors"), with no chart format to learn.
